fixes.current: Nationalists led by Messali Hadj flew this flag in the 1930s, and the National Liberation Front carried it through the war of independence. It became the national flag in 1962 and a law of April 1963 fixed its design but gave no meaning. Green is traditionally linked to Islam and white to peace and purity; red is often said to recall those who died for freedom, and the crescent and star are long-used symbols of Islam.
fixes.value: Nationalists led by Messali Hadj used this design from the 1930s, and the National Liberation Front carried it through the war of independence. It became the national flag in 1962, and a 1963 law fixed its design. Algeria's government says white stands for peace, green for hope and red for the value of work, and that the crescent and star show Islam is the main religion. Older readings link green to Islam and red to sacrifice.
fixes.reason: I opened the Algerian Ministry of Foreign Affairs state-symbols page (embassy site on mfa.gov.dz): it states white = peace, love and goodness; green = hope for progress and a better tomorrow; red = the importance of work in achieving prosperity; crescent and star = Islam is the main religion, and cites Law 63-145 of 25 April 1963. The shipped text presents only traditional readings and says no meaning is given, which is misleading now that an official government statement exists. The replacement states the government wording plainly, hedges the older readings, keeps the 1963 law clause, and is 430 characters with no jargon or double quotes.

fixes.current: Omar Faiek Shennib designed this flag for the kingdom of Libya, independent in 1951. The black band with a white crescent and star comes from the banner of the Senussi rulers of eastern Libya. Shennib said red recalls blood shed for freedom, black the dark years of Italian rule, green farming and future wealth, the crescent the Islamic calendar and the star hope. Replaced after 1969, it was brought back in the 2011 uprising.
fixes.value: Omar Faiek Shennib designed this flag for the kingdom of Libya in 1951. Its black band with a white crescent and star comes from the Senussi rulers' banner in eastern Libya. His daughters said he chose red for blood shed for freedom, black for the dark years of Italian rule and green for farming and future wealth. A kingdom-era booklet said the crescent marks the new Islamic month and the star means hope. Replaced in 1969, it returned in 2011.
fixes.reason: Both verifiers flagged the attribution and I confirmed it on the Flag of Libya article: the red, black and green meanings come from Shennib's daughters (2011 interviews), who said the crescent and star refer to the Senussi flag and King Idris; the crescent = start of the Islamic lunar month and star = hope meanings come from a Kingdom of Libya Ministry of Information booklet, not from Shennib. The shipped text wrongly credits the crescent and star meanings to Shennib. The replacement separates the two sources, keeps every feature explained, and is 447 characters, no jargon, no double quotes. Adoption 24 December 1951, abolition after the 1 September 1969 coup and 2011 readoption are confirmed on the same page.

fixes.current: The Roman city of Leptis Magna, east of Tripoli, was the birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus and is one of the best preserved Roman sites anywhere.
fixes.value: Leptis Magna, a Roman city east of Tripoli, was the birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus and is among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean.
fixes.reason: Both verifiers agree and I confirmed on the Leptis Magna article: the ruins are 130 km east of Tripoli, Septimius Severus was born in the city, and the sourced wording is 'among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean'. The shipped 'one of the best preserved Roman sites anywhere' is a worldwide superlative no source backs. Replacement is 157 characters, neutral and stable.

fixes.current: Sudan chose this flag in 1970 through a design competition won by artist Abdel Rahman Ahmed Al-Jali. Red, white, black and green are the Pan-Arab colors, laid out like the Arab Liberation flag that began in Egypt; the green triangle makes it Sudan's own. The colors are often read as red for struggle and sacrifice, white for peace, black for the country's name, which means land of the black people in Arabic, and green for Islam and farmland.
fixes.value: Sudan chose this flag in 1970 in a contest won by artist Abdel Rahman Ahmed Al-Jali. Red, white, black and green are the Pan-Arab colors, first combined in the 1916 Arab Revolt flag, and the stripes follow the Arab Liberation flag from Egypt; the green triangle makes it Sudan's own. The colors are often read as red for struggle, white for peace, black for the country's name (land of the black people in Arabic) and green for Islam and farmland.
fixes.reason: Field rule: a shared motif (Pan-Arab colors) must name its shared origin in one clause. The shipped text names the Arab Liberation layout from Egypt but never says where the four Pan-Arab colors come from. I confirmed on the Pan-Arab colors article that they were first combined in 1916 in the flag of the Arab Revolt, and on the Flag of Sudan article the 20 May 1970 adoption, the competition, the designer's name, the Arab Liberation Flag basis and the hedged color readings. Replacement is 447 characters, keeps all facts and hedging, no jargon, no double quotes. Low-stakes: the shipped text is otherwise accurate.

fixes.current: Cameroon chose three upright bands of green, red and yellow in 1957, the second country after Ghana to adopt these Pan-African colors. Red is usually read as the color of unity, and the gold star in the center is called the star of unity. Yellow is said to stand for the sun and the northern grasslands, green for the southern forests. Two stars marked the union of the former French and British parts from 1961 until one star was adopted in 1975.
fixes.value: Cameroon chose three upright bands of green, red and yellow in 1957, the second country after Ghana to use the Pan-African colors of Ethiopia's flag. Red is usually read as the color of unity, and the central gold star is called the star of unity. Yellow is said to stand for the sun and northern grasslands, green for southern forests. Two stars marked the union of the former French and British parts from 1961 until one star replaced them in 1975.
fixes.reason: Shared-motif rule: the Pan-African colors must name their shared origin in one clause; the current text names the motif but not where it comes from. Confirmed: the Pan-African colours article says the green-yellow-red combination was borrowed from the flag of Ethiopia and that Ghana was the first state to adopt it in 1957; the Flag of Cameroon article says Cameroon was the second state to adopt the colors (Law No. 46 of 26 October 1957), reports red as unity and the star of unity as readings rather than official meanings, two stars for East and West Cameroon from 1961, and the single star from 20 May 1975. Replacement counted at 450 characters, hedging unchanged, no jargon.

fixes.current: Barthélemy Boganda, its first leader, designed the flag, adopted on 1 December 1958. He said its colors stood for the four territories of French Equatorial Africa and for France: blue and white are often linked to France, green and yellow to the Pan-African colors. The red upright stripe is, in his words, the symbol of our blood. Blue is said to mean the sky and freedom, white peace, green hope, yellow tolerance, and the star a bright future.
fixes.value: Barthélemy Boganda, its first leader, designed the flag adopted on 1 December 1958. He said the colors stood for the four territories of French Equatorial Africa and for France: blue and white often linked to France, green and yellow to the Pan-African colors of Ethiopia's flag. The red upright stripe was, he said, the symbol of our blood. Blue is said to mean sky and freedom, white peace, green hope, yellow tolerance, the star a bright future.
fixes.reason: Same shared-motif rule. Confirmed against the Flag of the Central African Republic article: designed by Boganda, adopted 1 December 1958 by the Legislative Assembly of Ubangi-Shari, his quoted words on the four territories of French Equatorial Africa plus metropolitan France and the red stripe as the symbol of our blood, blue and white for France and green and yellow for Africa; the individual color and star meanings are cited only to Flagpedia and stay hedged. The Pan-African colours article lists the Central African Republic among flags with Pan-African symbolism and gives Ethiopia's flag as the origin of the green-yellow-red set. Replacement counted at 448 characters.

fixes.current: Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River drop about 105 meters across a curtain some 400 meters wide, making them one of Africa's largest waterfalls by volume.
fixes.value: Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River drop about 105 meters across a curtain some 400 meters wide and rank among Africa's largest waterfalls by volume.
fixes.reason: The current wording presents height and width as the cause of a large volume, which is a false link (volume depends on flow, not on drop or width), so it misleads. The Kalandula Falls article confirms the Lucala River, 105 m height, 400 m width and the statement that they are one of the largest waterfalls by volume in Africa (cited to a Malanje-Angola.com page and world-waterfalls.com). The replacement keeps every verified figure and states the volume ranking as a separate claim; 149 characters, no dated wording.

fixes.value: ["Light Blue","Yellow","Red"]
fixes.reason: Article 1 of the DRC constitution (2006, as amended 2011) describes the emblem as the sky-blue flag with a yellow star in the upper left corner; the Wikipedia flag article describes a sky blue field (#007FFF, Pantone 299) and says the 2006 change was from royal blue to sky blue; the shipped image /tmp/flagwork/out/cd.png is a bright azure, and the app's own flagDescription already says 'a lighter sky blue'. The catalog uses 'Light Blue' for the same shade on Botswana, Somalia, Djibouti, Argentina, Kazakhstan, Fiji and others, so 'Light Blue' is both accurate and consistent.

fixes.current: The flag dates from 15 September 1959, shortly before independence from France. Green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors shared with Ethiopia, and this is the only Pan-African flag to arrange them diagonally. Green was said to mean farming and forests, yellow the friendship and nobility of the people; red was given no meaning. A Marxist government flew a red flag from 1970 until the original returned on 10 June 1991.
fixes.value: The flag dates from 15 September 1959, shortly before independence from France. Green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors shared with Ethiopia, and this is the only Pan-African flag to arrange them diagonally. Green was said to mean farming and forests, yellow the friendship and nobility of the people; red was given no meaning. A Marxist government later replaced it with a red flag, and the original returned on 10 June 1991.
fixes.reason: The current text dates the red flag 'from 1970', but Britannica ('On December 30, 1969, a new Marxist regime altered the national flag') and Flags of the World ('abolished on 30 December 1969 when a new constitution introduced a Marxist one-party state') both place the change in 1969; only Wikipedia's infobox gives 2 January 1970, and even its body text implies the People's Republic was proclaimed in 1969. The replacement drops the contested year, keeps the restoration date of 10 June 1991 that all three sources share, and changes nothing else; 435 characters, one paragraph, no jargon.

UN WPP 2024 mid-2024 medium variant for Burkina Faso is 23,548,781 (confirmed on Worldometers' republication of WPP 2024; 2023 row 23,025,776 matches the Wikipedia UN list). The field rule rounds to 3 significant figures, or 4 when the third digit would be 5: 3 s.f. gives 23,500,000, so 4 s.f. applies and gives 23,550,000. The shipped 23,549,000 is a 5 s.f. value the rule does not allow; the no-trailing-5 clause only forbids 3-digit values.

fixes.current: The Kingdom of Dahomey, which ruled this land before the French, was famous for its elite units of female soldiers, known in Europe as the Dahomey Amazons.
fixes.value: The Kingdom of Dahomey, which ruled southern Benin before the French, was famous for its elite units of female soldiers, known in Europe as the Dahomey Amazons.
fixes.reason: Wikipedia's Dahomey article confirms the kingdom grew on the Abomey Plateau and expanded south to the Atlantic coast, covering about 10,000 km2 in 1700, a fraction of Benin's 114,763 km2; the north of present-day Benin was held by other polities. 'Ruled this land' implies the whole country, so 'southern Benin' is the accurate wording. The replacement is exactly 160 characters, one sentence, neutral, and will stay true; the Dahomey Amazons claim is confirmed in the same article.

fixes.current: Guinea adopted this flag on 10 November 1958, weeks after leaving French rule. The upright bands follow the French flag's layout, but the colors are the Pan-African red, yellow and green, taken from Ghana's 1957 flag. President Sékou Touré said red stands for the blood of those who died fighting colonial rule and for work, yellow for gold and the sun, and green for the land's plants, matching the motto Work, Justice, Solidarity.
fixes.value: Guinea adopted this flag on 10 November 1958, weeks after leaving French rule. Its upright bands copy the French flag, but the colors are the Pan-African red, yellow and green of Ethiopia and Ghana, also used by Guinea's independence party. President Sékou Touré said red stands for the blood of those who died fighting colonial rule and for work, yellow for gold and the sun, and green for its plants, echoing the motto Work, Justice, Solidarity.
fixes.reason: The current text states as plain fact that the colors were taken from Ghana's 1957 flag. Both Britannica (opened) and the Wikipedia flag article (opened) say Guinea's Democratic Party had already used red, yellow and green as early as 1954, before Ghana's flag existed; Wikipedia carries both the RDA/Ghana derivation and the 1954 PDG use without resolving them, and Britannica does not mention the RDA at all. The replacement names the Pan-African shared origin (Ethiopia, Ghana) and the party's prior use without asserting a direct borrowing from Ghana. Touré's meanings (sacrifice and labour; gold and sun; vegetation; mapped to the motto Work, Justice, Solidarity) are confirmed by both pages. 447 characters, one paragraph, no jargon, no double quotes, American spelling.

fixes.current: Liberia's flag dates from 24 August 1847 and was sewn by a committee of seven women. It resembles the US flag because Liberia was founded in 1822 as a settlement for free Black Americans. The eleven stripes are said to stand for the eleven signers of the Declaration of Independence, the white star for Africa's first republic, and the blue square for Africa. A 1961 law reads blue as liberty and justice, white as purity, red as courage.
fixes.value: Liberia's flag dates from 24 August 1847 and was sewn by a committee of seven women. It resembles the US flag because Liberia was founded in 1822 as a settlement for free Black Americans. The eleven stripes are said to stand for the eleven signers of Liberia's Declaration of Independence, the white star for Africa's first republic, and the blue square for Africa. A 1961 law reads blue as liberty and justice, white as purity, red as courage.
fixes.reason: Placed right after the sentence about the US flag and American settlers, 'the Declaration of Independence' reads as the US document; the stripes refer to the Liberian Declaration of Independence of 26 July 1847, signed by eleven delegates (plus a secretary). Adding 'Liberia's' removes the ambiguity. Wikipedia's flag article confirms the 24 August 1847 adoption, the seven-woman committee, and that the stripes symbolize the signatories of the Liberian Declaration of Independence; the declaration article lists eleven signing delegates. Replacement is 444 characters, one paragraph, no jargon, no double quotes, all other wording unchanged.

fixes.current: Mali's green, gold and red bands are the Pan-African colors also seen on the flags of Ghana, Guinea and Senegal. Mali took them up in 1959 while briefly united with Senegal; that flag had a black human figure, the kanaga, in the center. It was removed in March 1961 because many Muslims objected to a human image. Green is often said to stand for fertile land, gold for mineral wealth and red for blood shed for independence.
fixes.value: Mali's green, gold and red bands are the Pan-African colors also seen on the flags of Ghana, Guinea and Senegal. Mali took them up in 1959 while briefly united with Senegal; that flag had a black human figure, the kanaga, in the center. It was removed in March 1961 after some Muslims objected that a human image went against Islam. Green is often said to stand for fertile land, gold for mineral wealth and red for blood shed for independence.
fixes.reason: Both the Wikipedia flag article and Britannica (opened by me) attribute the removal of the kanaga to objections from Muslim fundamentalists who held that a human image was contrary to Islam, not to a broad popular objection; 'many Muslims objected' misstates who objected and omits the grounds. The replacement (446 characters, one paragraph, no jargon, American spelling) keeps every other verified claim and the hedged color meanings. [Edited after review: "strict Muslims" replaced by "some Muslims": says who objected and why without labelling them.]

fixes.current: The flag comes from a banner King Sobhuza II gave in 1941 to Swazi soldiers sent to the Second World War, and became the national flag at independence in 1968. Officially red stands for past battles, blue for peace and stability and yellow for natural resources. The black and white ox-hide shield shows black and white people living in peace, two spears mean protection, and the stick carries feather tassels that only the king may use.
fixes.value: The flag comes from a banner King Sobhuza II gave in 1941 to Swazi soldiers in the Second World War; first raised in 1967, it became the national flag in October 1968, just after independence. Officially red stands for past battles, blue for peace and yellow for resources. The black and white ox-hide shield shows black and white people living in peace, two spears mean protection, and the stick carries feather tassels that only the king may use.
fixes.reason: The current text says the flag became the national flag 'at independence in 1968', but it was first hoisted on 25 April 1967 (replacing the Union Jack, per Britannica) and was formally adopted on 6 October 1968, a month after independence on 6 September 1968; Britannica states no change was made on Independence Day. I confirmed both dates on Wikipedia's flag article and Britannica. All other claims (1941 banner, color meanings, shield, spears, king-only feather tassels) match Wikipedia's flag article. Replacement is 448 characters, one paragraph, no jargon or double quotes.

fixes.current: The coelacanth, a deep-sea fish once known only from fossils, was caught alive off the Comoros island of Anjouan in 1952 and still lives in its waters.
fixes.value: The coelacanth, a deep-sea fish thought extinct until 1938, was found again off the Comoros island of Anjouan in 1952 and still lives in Comorian waters.
fixes.reason: The current wording implies the 1952 Anjouan catch was the rediscovery of a fish known only from fossils; Wikipedia and Britannica both state the living coelacanth was first found in 1938 off South Africa and that the 1952 Anjouan fish was the second known specimen. Neither source supports 'caught alive'. The replacement keeps the Comoros angle, is accurate, neutral, undated in its statistics and 153 characters.

fixes.current: Adopted at independence in 1993 and standardized in 1995, the flag copies the red, green and blue triangles of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front flag of 1977. Red is officially for blood shed for independence, green for farming and herds, blue for the sea's wealth. The gold olive branch and wreath replaced the front's star and come from Eritrea's 1952 flag, which honored the United Nations. The 30 leaves are said to mark 30 years of war.
fixes.value: Adopted at independence in 1993 and standardized in 1995, the flag copies the red, green and blue triangles of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front flag of 1977. The government says red stands for blood shed for independence, green for farming and herds, blue for the sea's wealth. The gold olive branch and wreath replaced the front's star and come from Eritrea's 1952 flag, which honored the UN. The 30 leaves are said to mark 30 years of war.
fixes.reason: "Officially" implies the color meanings are fixed in law, but no proclamation or constitutional text gives them: the 1997 constitution only names the colors, Wikipedia's basis is a Ministry of Information (shabait.com) article, and Britannica attaches the red/green/blue meanings to the EPLF party flag of 1977 and does not restate them for the national flag. "The government says" states exactly what the opened sources support. All other claims verified against both sources (24 May 1993 first hoisting, 1995 leaf standardization, EPLF 1977 origin, star replaced by the olive emblem from the 1952 flag whose light blue honored the UN, 30 leaves for the years of war). 447 characters, one paragraph, no double quotes.

fixes.current: Madagascar adopted its flag in 1958, when it gained self-rule from France, two years before independence. Red and white were the colors of the Merina kingdom, which ruled much of the island in the 1800s, linking the new nation to its past. Green is often said to stand for the coastal peoples and for hope. At the 1958 ceremony white was called purity and red sovereignty, but the constitution only describes the bands, with no official meaning.
fixes.value: Madagascar adopted its flag in 1958, when it gained self-rule from France, two years before independence. Red and white were the colors of the Merina kingdom, which ruled much of the island in the 1800s, linking the new nation to its past. Green is often said to stand for the coastal regions and for hope. At the 1958 ceremony white was called purity and red sovereignty, but the constitution only describes the bands, with no official meaning.
fixes.reason: Britannica's wording is that green "represents the coastal regions and symbolizes hope"; the flag's Wikipedia article ties green to hope (the 1958 Tsara statement and the presidency's reading) and to the island's vegetation, and neither source links it to the coastal peoples as a group. "Coastal regions" is the reading the sources actually give. Everything else verified: adoption 21 October 1958 one week after autonomy on 14 October 1958, red and white as Merina royal colors, the 1958 statement (white purity, red sovereignty), and the 2010 constitution's Article 4 describing the layout only. 445 characters, no double quotes.

fixes.current: Mauritius adopted its flag at independence in 1968; retired schoolteacher Gurudutt Moher designed it. A 2022 national symbols law gives the official meanings: red for the struggle for freedom and independence, blue for the Indian Ocean around the island, yellow for the light of freedom shining over it, and green for farmland that stays green all year. The colors are also often said to match the four main political parties of the time.
fixes.value: Mauritius adopted its flag at independence on 12 March 1968; primary school teacher Gurudutt Moher designed it. Mauritian flag law gives the official meanings: red for the struggle for freedom and independence, blue for the Indian Ocean around the island, yellow for the new light of independence, and green for farmland that stays green all year. The four colors are also often said to match the four main political parties of the time.
fixes.reason: Confirmed: Moher was a working primary school teacher when he designed the flag (ozoutback: 'was a primary school teacher at that time'); Wikipedia calls him retired only at his death in 2017 aged 93. The official meanings come from the schedule of the National Flag Act 2015 (Act No. 26 of 2015) as quoted verbatim by FOTW, where yellow is 'the new light of independence'; Wikipedia cites the 2022 Act only for the flag's description and color shades, and the 2022 bill text could not be opened (404), so the law's year is dropped. 437 characters, one paragraph, no jargon.

fixes.current: Adopted in 1983, the flag grew out of that of FRELIMO, which won independence from Portugal in 1975. The constitution gives the meanings: green for the land, black for Africa, yellow for mineral wealth, white lines for peace, the red triangle for the fight against colonial rule, the star for solidarity with other peoples, the book for education, the hoe for farming and the AK-47 rifle for defense. In 2005 parliament voted to keep the rifle.
fixes.value: Adopted in 1983, the flag grew out of that of FRELIMO, which won independence from Portugal in 1975. The constitution gives the meanings: green for the land, black for Africa, yellow for mineral wealth, white lines for peace, the red triangle for the fight against colonial rule, the star for solidarity with other peoples, the book for study, the hoe for work and the gun, shown as an AK-47, for defense. In 2005 parliament voted to keep the flag.
fixes.reason: Confirmed against Article 297 of the constitution at constituteproject.org: it says 'a crossed hoe and gun' (never rifle or AK-47) and that 'the book, the hoe and the gun shall symbolise study, production and defence'. The AK-47 identification is a general understanding (Wikipedia), so the text now attributes it as how the gun is shown rather than as the constitution's wording. The 2005 vote (155 to 79) was against changing the flag as a whole after a redesign competition, not a vote on the rifle alone. Adoption on 1 May 1983 and FRELIMO origin confirmed. 448 characters, one paragraph, neutral on the rifle per the owner rule.

fixes.current: Adopted in 1996 after multiparty politics returned, this flag mixes the colors of the two main parties: blue and yellow from the Democratic Party, red, white and green from the ruling party. Officially the five bands spreading from the lower left corner show a young country moving into the future. Blue is the sky and sea, yellow the sun, red the people working in unity and love, white social justice and harmony, green the land and nature.
fixes.value: Adopted in 1996 as multiparty rule returned, this flag mixes the colors of the main parties of that time: blue and yellow from the Democratic Party, red, white and green from the People's Progressive Front, which had ruled since 1977. Officially the bands fanning out from the lower left corner show a young country moving ahead. Blue is sky and sea, yellow the sun, red the people working in unity, white social justice and harmony, green the land.
fixes.reason: 'the ruling party' is volatile wording that already went stale: the party that supplied red, white and green (SPUP, renamed Seychelles People's Progressive Front 1978, Parti Lepep 2009, United Seychelles 2018) ruled 1977-2020, lost the presidency in 2020 and only returned in October 2025 (Wikipedia United Seychelles, opened). The replacement names the party by its 1996 name with a past-tense anchor, keeps the official colour and band meanings exactly as quoted on Wikipedia Flag of Seychelles, uses no jargon, and is 449 characters (I shortened the verifier's text, whose 'in power since 1977' still reads as present tense).

fixes.current: Senegal adopted this flag in 1960 on leaving the short-lived Mali Federation. It kept the federation's three bands of green, gold and red, the Pan-African colors, but swapped its black human figure for a green star. The government says green stands for hope and faith, gold for wealth earned by work and for the arts, red for life and the sacrifice of the nation, and the star's five points for openness to the five continents.
fixes.value: Senegal adopted this flag in 1960 on leaving the Mali Federation. It kept the federation's three bands of green, gold and red, the Pan-African colors first flown by Ethiopia, but swapped its black human figure for a green star. The government says green stands for hope and faith, gold for wealth earned by work and for the arts, red for life and the sacrifice of the nation, and the star's five points for openness to the five continents.
fixes.reason: Shared-motif consistency: the decided texts for Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Guinea, Ghana, Ethiopia and Congo all name Ethiopia as the origin of the Pan-African colors; Senegal names the motif but not the origin. Minimal edit, 439 characters.

fixes.current: Artist Paul Ahyi designed the flag, adopted on 27 April 1960, the day Togo became independent from France. Its green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors. Its five bands are often said to stand for the five regions. The presidency explains green as forests, farming and hope, yellow as natural resources, faith and maturity, the red square as the blood of independence fighters, and the white star as peace, light and intelligence.
fixes.value: Paul Ahyi designed the flag, adopted on 27 April 1960, the day Togo became independent from France. Its green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors of Ethiopia's flag. The five bands are often said to be the five regions. The presidency explains green as forests, farming and hope, yellow as natural resources, faith and maturity, the red square as the blood of independence fighters, and the white star as peace, light and intelligence.
fixes.reason: Shared-motif consistency: names the shared origin (Ethiopia) in one clause like the other Pan-African entries. 442 characters.

fixes.current: Adopted at independence from Portugal in 1975 and based on the flag of the MLSTP, the movement that won independence; its leader and first president, Manuel Pinto da Costa, is credited with the design. Green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors shared by many African flags, used here to recall the independence movement. The president's office says the red triangle stands for equality and the two black stars for the two main islands.
fixes.value: Adopted at independence from Portugal in 1975 and based on the flag of the MLSTP, the movement that won independence; its leader and first president, Manuel Pinto da Costa, is credited with the design. Green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors of Ethiopia's flag, used here to recall the independence movement. The president's office says the red triangle stands for equality and the two black stars for the two main islands.
fixes.reason: Shared-motif consistency: names Ethiopia as the origin of the Pan-African colors like the other entries. The symbolism (presidency: triangle for equality, stars for the two islands) matches Wikipedia's flag article. 432 characters.

ownerDecisions.issue: The shipped capital string 'Ciudad de la Paz (capital), Malabo (former capital)' matches neither the owner decision for this audit ('Malabo, Ciudad de la Paz' with quizCapital 'Ciudad de la Paz') nor the seed ownerRules (Malabo only); the facts are that a decree-law of 2 January 2026 declared Ciudad de la Paz the capital with institutions still moving and Bata the largest city, so the owner should settle which string ships (quizCapital 'Ciudad de la Paz' is contained in both the shipped and the owner strings and needs no change).

editedAfterReview.proposedValue: Mali's green, gold and red bands are the Pan-African colors also seen on the flags of Ghana, Guinea and Senegal. Mali took them up in 1959 while briefly united with Senegal; that flag had a black human figure, the kanaga, in the center. It was removed in March 1961 after strict Muslims objected that a human image went against Islam. Green is often said to stand for fertile land, gold for mineral wealth and red for blood shed for independence.
